explanations.answer: Turn in an account because you cannot be manager any longer
explanations.explanation: That's exactly it, baker. The rich man says, "What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) He asks for the books and the job is gone in the same breath. No warning shot, no second chance, just "hand me the paperwork."

explanations.answer: Pay back everything you wasted by the end of the week
explanations.explanation: I get why this one tempts you, because a boss wanting his money back makes sense. But the master never mentions repayment or a deadline. He says, "Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) The first thing he asks for is the books, and the second thing is the manager's job.

explanations.answer: Take a smaller job until you earn back my trust
explanations.explanation: A demotion would've been a soft landing, friend, and I wish the manager had gotten one. The master says no such thing. He says, "…you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) The position is simply taken away.

Close, but the manager rules both of those out. He says, "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) So the shovel and the cup are both off the table. He needs a third idea, and he's about to find one.

Right, baker. The manager says, "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) He names both options and crosses them off in one sentence. That's a man with no shovel, no cup, and a lot of thinking to do.

explanations.answer: So people will welcome him into their homes
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The manager says, "I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) He's already planning for the day after the job ends. Say what you want about him, the man does not sit around waiting.

explanations.answer: So his master will give him the job back
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice ending, but the manager never says it. His plan is for "after my removal from management," so he's already treating the job as gone. (Luke 16:4) What he wants is for people to welcome him into their homes.

explanations.answer: So he can pay off his own debts
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since this whole story is full of debts. But the manager's own debts never come up. He says his plan is so that "people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) The debts in this story belong to the master's debtors.

explanations.answer: Sit down quickly and write fifty
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The manager tells him, "Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) A hundred measures of olive oil becomes fifty. Notice the "quickly," too. This man is not asking for a second opinion.

explanations.answer: Pay the full hundred by tomorrow
explanations.explanation: Nope, the manager goes the other direction. He says, "Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) Nobody is asked to pay by tomorrow. The debtor walks away owing half of what he came in with.

explanations.answer: Double the amount to two hundred
explanations.explanation: Whoa, friend, that would make for a very short list of new friends. The manager tells the debtor to "write fifty," not two hundred. (Luke 16:6) The bill goes down by half, and that's how a manager makes people glad to see him.

Right on, baker. The second debtor owes a hundred measures of wheat, and the manager says, "Take your bill and write eighty." (Luke 16:7) Each debtor gets a different number. Fifty for the first, eighty for the second.
Ninety is a nice round number, but it's not the one in the text. The manager tells the debtor, "Take your bill and write eighty." (Luke 16:7) That's the number to remember for this second debtor.
Close, friend, but seventy is too generous. The manager says, "Take your bill and write eighty." (Luke 16:7) And this debtor owes wheat, not oil, so don't mix him up with the first one.

explanations.answer: He commends him for acting shrewdly
explanations.explanation: That's the twist, baker. "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) I was ready for fireworks and got a compliment instead. The text still calls him the dishonest manager, so the story is praising his shrewdness, not his honesty.

explanations.answer: He has him thrown into prison
explanations.explanation: Honestly, I'd have bet on this one too. But the text says, "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) No prison, no shouting, just a commendation. That's what makes this story so surprising.

explanations.answer: He makes him repay the difference
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, friend, since the master lost money here. But the text never mentions repayment. It says, "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) The master's response is a commendation.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) It's a comparison, and the sons of light come out second. I think that's worth a quiet moment of thinking.

It does sound like something that couldn't be in there, friend, but it is. Jesus says, "For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) So the sons of this age are the ones called more shrewd in that comparison.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves…" (Luke 16:9) The manager used his master's bills to make friends, and now Jesus talks about worldly wealth the same way. Money in your hands can be put to work for people.

explanations.answer: To build bigger barns for themselves
explanations.explanation: That's the rich fool's plan in another story, friend. In Jesus' words here, it's, "…use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves…" (Luke 16:9) Bigger barns aren't in this passage at all. Friends are.

explanations.answer: To buy more land for themselves
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but there's no land-buying in this passage. Jesus says, "…use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves…" (Luke 16:9) The goal he names is friends, not property.

That's right, baker. Jesus says to use worldly wealth to make friends "so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) Notice the "when it is gone." The wealth runs out, and the welcome doesn't.

It might sound too good to be true, friend, but it's what Jesus says. He tells them to use worldly wealth to make friends "so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) The money is gone, and the welcome is into eternal dwellings.

I see why you picked it, but it's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says, "…whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much." (Luke 16:10) The small thing tells you about the big thing. A dishonest little cookie leads to a dishonest big box.

Right, baker. Jesus says, "Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much." (Luke 16:10) So being dishonest with little doesn't prepare you to be honest with much. It goes the other direction.

That's it, baker. Jesus asks, "So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?" (Luke 16:11) Worldly wealth comes first, and true riches come after. He sets it up like a step.
That line is from a different parable, friend. In Luke 19:17 a master tells a servant, "…take charge of ten cities." In this passage, Jesus asks who will entrust you with "true riches." (Luke 16:11)

Good memory, but that phrase belongs to another moment. Jesus says to Peter, one of His disciples, "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven…" (Matthew 16:19) Here the question is about who will entrust you with "true riches." (Luke 16:11)

Yes, baker. Jesus asks, "And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) Faithfulness with what belongs to somebody else comes before getting something that's yours.

I can see why master jumped out, since it's all over this story. But Jesus says, "…who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) The word is own. Belongings of another, then belongings of your own.

Neighbor sounds friendly, friend, but it's not in this verse. Jesus asks, "…who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) The contrast is between belongings of another and belongings of your own.

I get it, baker, but Jesus says the opposite. "Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." (Luke 16:13) Loving both the same isn't one of the options. Two masters pull in two directions.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." (Luke 16:13) He lays out two outcomes, and equal love for both isn't one of them.

You nailed it, baker. Jesus ends with, "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13) The whole passage has been talking about wealth, and this is where He lands it. Two masters, and those are the two.

Caesar, the Roman emperor, does come up with Jesus in another place, friend. There He says, "Give back to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's." (Mark 12:17) But here Jesus says, "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13)

Baal, a false god, shows up in Elijah's story, when the prophet asks Israel, "How long will you waver between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21) But that's not this passage. Here Jesus says, "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13)
